Tal Fisher Tal Fisher share הקישור הועתק! 8 November 2026 | 6 minutes Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Hepatitis B is a disease caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which infects liver cells. Some people infected with the virus recover completely, while in others, the infection becomes chronic and can persist for many years. Chronic hepatitis B often causes no noticeable symptoms, but over time it can cause serious liver damage and lead to cirrhosis or even liver cancer. The disease is widespread: according to the World Health Organization, approximately 240 million people worldwide currently live with chronic hepatitis B. Existing antiviral treatments can suppress viral replication and reduce the risk of liver damage and serious complications, but they generally cannot eliminate the virus completely or fully stop the production of viral proteins. In a recent study, published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering, researchers investigated a novel approach to treating chronic hepatitis B. They used a technique designed to silence viral genes, preventing them from producing the proteins the virus needs to function and reproduce. The results were promising: mice carrying HBV and treated with the new method showed a substantial and sustained reduction in viral markers. The experimental treatment has also entered Phase 1/2 clinical trials in humans, with the first patient receiving it in January 2026. However, results establishing its safety or effectiveness in humans are not yet available. If proven safe and effective, the approach could eventually offer a new treatment option for people living with chronic hepatitis B. HBV infects liver cells and delivers its genetic material into their nuclei. Illustration of the liver and the hepatitis B virus | KATERYNA KON / Science Photo Library A Virus That Won’t Leave Viruses are tiny infectious agents that contain genetic material enclosed in a protein coat and cannot reproduce on their own. Once inside a host cell, they hijack its machinery to produce viral proteins and replicate their genetic material, ultimately generating new viruses. Viruses differ in several ways, including the type of genetic material they carry: some have DNA, while others have RNA. In our cells, DNA serves as a kind of recipe book, containing instructions for producing RNA molecules. Some of these RNA molecules then serve as templates for protein production.DNA is stored in the cell nucleus, while RNA molecules carrying instructions for protein production leave the nucleus and travel to ribosomes, where they serve as templates for synthesizing proteins. Viruses also rely on these basic processes, although where their genetic material is found and how it is copied and expressed vary from one virus to another. HBV is a DNA virus that infects liver cells and delivers its genetic material into their nuclei. There, the viral DNA is converted into a stable, circular form that remains in the nucleus and serves as a template for producing viral RNA. The cell then uses this RNA to manufacture the viral proteins needed to produce new viruses. During infection, some viral DNA may also become integrated into the DNA of the host cell. Once integrated, the viral sequences are copied along with the cell’s own DNA whenever it divides, making them difficult to eliminate without destroying the cell. Although this integrated DNA generally cannot produce complete, infectious HBV particles, it can continue to serve as a source of viral RNA and proteins. As a result, even when antiviral treatments suppress viral replication, infected cells may continue producing certain viral proteins. Existing and New Treatments Chronic HBV infection is commonly treated with drugs called nucleos(t)ide analogues, or NUCs. These drugs interfere with viral DNA replication, suppress the production of new viruses, and reduce the risk of liver disease progression. However, they generally do not eliminate the circular viral DNA that persists in the nuclei of infected cells or completely stop the production of viral proteins. As a result, treatment with NUCs is usually long-term and generally does not eliminate the infection. In the ongoing clinical trial, the experimental treatment is being administered alongside conventional antiviral therapy. In the new study, researchers investigated a different approach that takes advantage of a natural cellular process called DNA methylation. This process involves attaching small chemical groups, known as methyl groups, to DNA, which can affect gene activity. Methylation of certain regions of HBV DNA can suppress viral gene expression and reduce the production of viral RNA. To harness this mechanism, the researchers developed an experimental treatment called CRMA-1001. The treatment uses CRISPR technology, which allows scientists to target specific DNA sequences with high precision. While CRISPR is commonly used to cut DNA, in this case the researchers combined it with a system that adds methyl groups to specific regions of HBV DNA, suppressing viral gene expression without cutting the DNA itself. In the new study, researchers propose a different treatment approach that takes advantage of a naturally occurring cellular process called DNA methylation. During methylation, chemical groups known as methyl groups are added to DNA, affecting how it functions. In certain regions, methylation of HBV DNA can suppress its activity and reduce RNA production. To harness this phenomenon, the researchers developed an experimental treatment called CRMA-1001. The treatment is based on CRISPR technology, which enables precise targeting of specific sites in DNA. CRISPR is typically used to cut DNA, but in this case, it was coupled with a system designed to methylate regions of HBV DNA, with the aim of suppressing viral activity. In the study, researchers substantially reduced the amount of viral DNA circulating in the blood of treated mice. A blood test measuring HBV viral load | bangoland / Shutterstock Silencing the Virus The researchers tested the treatment in mice using several experimental approaches. In one experiment, in which viral DNA was integrated into the mice’s own DNA, a single dose of the treatment substantially reduced viral levels, an effect that persisted for seven months. In another experiment, which examined viral DNA that remained separate from the host cells’ DNA, three doses administered approximately one month apart produced even more striking results. Six months after treatment began, viral levels in approximately 90 percent of the mice that received a high dose had fallen below the level that the test could reliably measure. These findings suggest that the treatment may have long-lasting effects rather than merely temporarily suppressing viral activity. Following the experiments in mice, and before beginning clinical trials in humans, the researchers evaluated the treatment’s safety in monkeys, whose physiology is more similar to that of humans. Overall, the treatment did not appear to cause unintended changes in gene activity or interfere with the function of the monkeys’ own DNA. However, a temporary increase in liver enzyme levels raised questions that will require further investigation before the treatment can be tested more widely in humans. The study presents a promising new approach to treating chronic hepatitis B. It is important to remember, however, that a safe and effective vaccine is already available to prevent HBV infection. The vaccine cannot treat an infection that has already occurred, and this is where the new approach could make a difference: it is designed to help people who are already living with chronic hepatitis B. If clinical trials establish that the treatment is safe and effective in humans, it could eventually offer a new option for managing chronic hepatitis B. Although the research is still at an early stage, the findings are encouraging. The study illustrates how a deeper understanding of fundamental molecular processes can potentially lead to development of innovative medical treatments. By combining knowledge of how HBV operates within infected cells with advances in molecular technology, the researchers developed a way to suppress viral activity by silencing its DNA, rather than simply blocking viral replication, as existing treatments do. news.content_title: Hepatitis B Functional Cure Persists Off Treatment After Bepirovirsen
news.content: Hepatitis B functional cure with bepirovirsen held in 90% to 92% of responders 48 weeks after stopping all therapy, per data at The Liver Meeting 2026. A hepatitis B functional cure achieved with 24 weeks of bepirovirsen (Hibsago; GSK) was maintained by about 9 in 10 responders through 48 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B virus (HBV) treatment, according to end-of-study results from the phase 3 B-Well 1 and 2 trials presented at The Liver Meeting 2026 . 1 Two other presentations at the meeting modeled response in patients with lower antigen levels and laid out a US care pathway for delivering finite therapy. 2,3 Among patients who achieved functional cure, stopped nucleos(t)ide analogues, and completed follow-up, 90% and 92% maintained the response at week 96, 48 weeks after all HBV treatment ended. | Image credit: Vitalii Vodolazskyi - stock.adobe.com The data arrive weeks after the FDA approved bepirovirsen on October 20, 2026, as the first antisense oligonucleotide for chronic HBV infection. 4 It is indicated in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy for adults without cirrhosis who have received NA therapy for at least 6 months, have suppressed HBV DNA, and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3000 IU/mL or less as determined by an FDA-authorized test. 4 About 1.7 million people in the United States live with chronic HBV, according to GSK. 4 Standard NA therapy suppresses the virus but is typically taken indefinitely. Functional cure, defined in the B-Well trials as at least 24 weeks of sustained undetectable HBV DNA and HBsAg loss after finite therapy, is described by the investigators as the treatment goal in chronic HBV. 1 “Current care pathways for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) relying on long-term viral suppression deliver minimal functional cure (FC) rates,” wrote the authors of the US care pathway. 3 B-Well 1 ( NCT05630807 ) and B-Well 2 ( NCT05630820 ) were global, double-blind trials in adults without cirrhosis whose HBV was suppressed on NA therapy and whose HBsAg was above 100 IU/mL and at or below 3000 IU/mL. 1 Patients were randomly assigned 2:1 to bepirovirsen 300 mg or placebo weekly for 24 weeks, and eligible patients discontinued NAs at week 48. The primary outcome was functional cure at week 72. The pivotal results were previously presented at the European Association for the Study of the Liver Congress 2026 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine . 5 At week 72, 20% (127 of 650) of patients receiving bepirovirsen in B-Well 1 and 19% (106 of 570) in B-Well 2 achieved functional cure, compared with no patients receiving placebo. 1 About 24% of patients receiving bepirovirsen entered the durability stage after week 72. Among patients who stopped NAs, achieved functional cure at week 72, and completed week 96, 90% (114 of 127) in B-Well 1 and 92% (97 of 105) in B-Well 2 had a durable response, and similar durability was seen among those with baseline HBsAg of 1000 IU/mL or less. One patient who stopped NAs had a viral relapse and restarted NA therapy after week 72. Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. From weeks 73 to 96, the most common adverse events (AEs) were upper respiratory tract infection (4%), decreased creatinine renal clearance (2%), and nasopharyngitis (2%). Treatment-related AEs in that period occurred in 2% of patients and were single events. The investigators said bepirovirsen “had an acceptable safety profile without any evidence of latent safety concerns associated with prior [bepirovirsen] treatment.” Because the B-Well trials did not enroll patients with HBsAg below 100 IU/mL, GSK investigators used model-based extrapolation from 1194 B-Well participants benchmarked against 2067 patients in the real-world Everest study of pegylated interferon to estimate response in that group. 2 Functional cure rates in B-Well rose as baseline HBsAg fell, reaching 40% in the 100 to 200 IU/mL subgroup. The final model predicted mean functional cure rates of approximately 46% to 53% with 24 weeks of bepirovirsen in NA-treated patients with baseline HBsAg below 100 IU/mL, with the lower bound of the model’s 95% CI suggesting at least a 34% rate of functional cure in this patient population. Notably, the low-HBsAg estimates are model predictions, not trial results, and were produced by GSK, the drug’s manufacturer. A multidisciplinary panel of US clinicians, pharmacists, and advocates used a nominal group technique across 2 consensus meetings in 2026 to adapt a 9-step global care pathway proposed in 2025. 3 The first meeting, mainly of nonspecialists, produced a 6-step pathway, and the second, mainly of specialists, expanded it to 8 steps, each with 100% consensus. The final pathway separates shared decision-making at the start and end of treatment and adds detail to monitoring. Panelists identified quantitative HBsAg testing, access to functional cure treatment, patient engagement and adherence tools, provider education, care coordinators, and community awareness as priorities for implementation. “The new 8-step US FC pathway and implementation priorities may help guide the paradigm shift in CHB management from chronic viral suppression to finite FC therapy,” the authors concluded. 3 1. Paper presented at: The Liver Meeting 2026; November 5-9, 2026; Denver, Colorado. Abstract 0266. 2. Whittaker D, Desikan R, Renardy M, Paff M, Theodore D, Nader A. Predicting functional cure response with bepirovirsen in patients with baseline HBsAg levels < 100 IU/mL. Late-breaking abstract presented at: The Liver Meeting 2026; November 5-9, 2026; Denver, Colorado. Abstract 5024. 3. Ahn J, Caracostis A, Choi C, et al. New clinical care pathway in era of HBV functional cure: a US multidisciplinary expert consensus. Poster presented at: The Liver Meeting 2026; November 5-9, 2026; Denver, Colorado. Abstract 4144. 4. Accessed November 6, 2026. https://www.gsk.com/media/alvmln3q/final-2-_bepi_us_approval_sea_201026.pdf 5. Steinzor P. news.content_title: FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment
news.content: FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment The US FDA has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, for treating chronic hepatitis B in certain adults without cirrhosis. First-in-class: Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B. Eligible patients: Adults without cirrhosis who have received HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months.Patients must have suppressed HBV levels and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of ≤3,000 IU/mL, confirmed by an FDA-authorised test.This approval introduces a novel antisense-based treatment approach for selected patients with chronic hepatitis B, complementing existing antiviral therapy. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements. Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review. The approval was granted to GSK plc. This marks the first approval of an antisense oligonucleotide for this condition. The treatment is designed for patients who have received antiviral therapy for at least six months and have suppressed HBV levels and HBsAg levels of ≤3,000 IU/mL. news.content_zh: 2026年11月7日,美国FDA批准Hibsago(贝匹罗韦森)注射液与现有的抗病毒药物疗法联合用于治疗无肝硬化成人慢性乙型肝炎。这标志着反义寡核苷酸首次获得批准用于治疗这种疾病。治疗 专为接受 抗病毒药物 治疗至少六个月且 HBV 水平和 HBsAg 水平抑制≤3,000 IU/mL 的患者而设计。临床试验表明,接受 Hibsago 治疗的患者中有 24% 符合停止现有药物的标准,而接受安慰剂治疗的患者则没有。治疗 治疗 24 周后,接受 Hibsago 治疗的患者中有 19% 的病毒仍得到控制,血液中检测不到 HBsAg。FDA 已针对严重肝脏反应、血小板计数低和其他风险发出黑框警告,要求定期进行血液检查并与医疗保健提供者进行随访。该批准已授予 GSK plc,包括快速通道、突破性疗法和优先审评资格。这代表了管理 慢性乙型肝炎 的重要进步。

news.content: Menu SECTIONS News Features CME Conferences Clinical Tools Special Collections Multimedia Fact Sheets Diagnosis & Disease Info Topics Abdominal Infections Bone and Joint Infections Cardiovascular Infections Central Nervous System Infections Covid 19 News & Insights Eye Infections Gastrointestinal Infections General Infectious Disease General Medicine Hepatitis HIV/AIDS Infection Control and Prevention Nosocomial Infections Pleuropulmonary and Bronchial Infections Practice Management Reproductive Organ Infections and Sexually Transmitted Infections Sepsis Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Upper Respiratory Tract Infections Urinary Tract Infection Vector-Borne Illnesses Haymarket Medical Network Cancer Therapy Advisor Cardiology Advisor Clinical Advisor Clinical Pain Advisor Dermatology Advisor Endocrinology Advisor Gastroenterology Advisor Hematology Advisor Infectious Disease Advisor Medical Bag MPR Neurology Advisor Obesity Advisor Oncology Nurse Advisor Ophthalmology Advisor Optometry Advisor Psychiatry Advisor Pulmonology Advisor Rare Disease Advisor Renal and Urology News Rheumatology Advisor Sleep Wake Advisor Vaccine Advisor Search for: COVID-19 News CME Drugs Calculators Charts Resources Multimedia Meetings Part of the News and Features CME Conferences Clinical Tools Special Collections Multimedia Share this article Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Bluesky Share by Email Print Hepatitis Suboptimal Hepatitis B Vaccination Rates in US Liver Transplant Recipients Todd Neale, MA | Publish Date November 9, 2026 Older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, and lower educational attainment are associated with a decreased likelihood of receiving the hepatitis B vaccine prior to liver transplantation, highlighting the need for targeted interventions. In the United States, a substantial proportion of liver transplant recipients do not receive hepatitis B vaccination, according to study findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. Vaccination against hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a key part of preventing adverse outcomes in patients with all types of chronic liver disease, including those undergoing transplantation, and is recommended in clinical guidelines for those being considered for a new organ. Researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study to examine HBV vaccine coverage using data from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), which requires all liver transplant programs to report HBV serologies and vaccination history for transplant recipients before the procedure. The analysis included 13,851 adults who received a liver from a deceased donor between September 2022 and June 2024. Multilevel interventions and the utilization of a more immunogenic vaccine may improve vaccination rates in this population. Overall, 59.9% of patients were considered vaccinated based on self-reported receipt of HBV vaccine (43.7%) and/or a positive anti-HB antibody test (38.6%). Compared with unvaccinated patients, vaccinated patients were more likely to be women (39.2% vs 36.2%), to have at least a high school education (91.7% vs 84.9%), and to have spent more than 6 months on the transplant waitlist (24.5% vs 20.1%). They also had higher rates of hepatitis C virus infection (3.8% vs 3.1%) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; 19.9% vs 18.1%). Vaccinated patients also had a lower median age (56 vs 57 years) and median model for end-stage liver disease-sodium (MELD-Na) score at the time of UNOS listing (21 vs 23). In multivariate logistic regression analyses, positive predictors of HBV vaccination were as follows: Having a bachelor’s degree or higher (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.09; 95% CI, 1.06-1.12); Black race (aOR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.02-1.14); HCC diagnosis (aOR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.10); Waitlist time of more than 6 months (aOR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.11); and, Female sex (aOR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.02-1.08). Conversely, older patients and those with alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), other liver etiologies, a MELD-Na score of 30 or greater, and less than a high school education were less likely to be vaccinated. Vaccination rates varied across UNOS regions, tending to be higher in the Northeast and Northwest and lower in the Southeast. Study limitations include the lack of information on anti-HB antibody titer levels and potential confounders such as income and immigration status; the inability to assess factors such as variability in provider recommendations, vaccine hesitancy, and access to vaccination; and missing data for nontransplanted waitlist candidates. According to the researchers, “Multilevel interventions and the utilization of a more immunogenic vaccine may improve vaccination rates in this population.” They added, “Target interventions should focus on older adults, patients with ALD, and higher MELD-Na, while also addressing regional and educational disparities.” References: Shi MA, Han J, Albahra R, et al. Hepatitis B vaccination for liver transplant recipients in the United States: a national cohort study. Clin Infect Dis. Published online September 29, 2026. doi:10.1093/cid/ciag585

analysis.event: A retrospective cohort study found that suboptimal hepatitis B vaccination rates were observed among liver transplant recipients in the US, with 59.9% considered vaccinated based on self-reported receipt of HBV vaccine and/or a positive anti-HB antibody test.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study identified disparities in vaccination rates, with older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, and lower educational attainment associated with decreased vaccination likelihood. Vaccinated patients had lower median age and MELD-Na scores and higher rates of hepatitis C virus infection and hepatocellular carcinoma.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study highlights the need for targeted interventions to improve vaccination rates, particularly among older adults, patients with ALD, and those with higher MELD-Na scores. It also notes regional and educational disparities in vaccination rates.

Overall, 59.9% of patients were considered vaccinated based on self-reported receipt of the hepatitis B vaccine (43.7%) and/or a positive anti-HB antibody test (38.6%). They also had higher rates of hepatitis C virus infection and hepatocellular carcinoma compared to unvaccinated patients. The study noted that vaccination rates varied across UNOS regions, with higher rates in the Northeast and Northwest and lower rates in the Southeast. Researchers emphasized the need for multilevel interventions and the use of more immunogenic vaccines to address disparities, particularly among older adults, patients with alcohol-associated liver disease, and those with higher MELD-Na scores.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 9 月 29 日发表在《临床传染病》上的一项研究发现,乙型肝炎 疫苗接种 率不理想在美国肝移植受者中很常见。研究人员利用 2022 年 9 月至 2024 年 6 月的数据,分析了 13,851 名接受已故捐赠者肝脏移植的成年人。总体而言,根据自我报告的乙型肝炎 疫苗 (43.7%) 和/或抗 HB 抗体检测呈阳性 (38.6%),59.9% 的患者被认为已接种疫苗。接种疫苗的患者更有可能是女性、受教育程度较高且在移植等候名单上停留超过 6 个月。与未接种疫苗的患者相比,他们的丙型肝炎病毒感染和肝细胞癌的发生率也更高。研究指出,UNOS 地区的 疫苗接种 比率有所不同,东北部和西北部的比率较高,东南部的比率较低。研究人员强调需要采取多层次干预措施并使用更具免疫原性的 疫苗 来解决差异,特别是在老年人、酒精相关性肝病患者和 MELD-Na 评分较高的患者中。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Distinct proteomic patterns link hepatitis B treatments to HBsAg decline by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Distinct proteomic patterns link hepatitis B treatments to HBsAg decline Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have identified distinct longitudinal plasma proteomic trajectories associated with two different immunomodulatory therapies for chronic hepatitis B, suggesting that specific protein changes may correlate with favorable treatment responses. The study, published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology, examined how pegylated interferon-alpha (PEG-IFNα) and PD-1 blockade alter the circulating inflammatory proteome in patients whose viral replication is already suppressed by nucleos(t)ide analogues. By profiling plasma samples over a 24-week period, the team found that while both therapies induce immune remodeling, the breadth and timing of these changes differ significantly between the two treatment modalities. The investigation focused on 25 patients with chronic hepatitis B who were receiving either PD-1 blockade or PEG-IFNα therapy. The cohort was divided into two groups: ten patients received PD-1 blockade, and fifteen patients received PEG-IFNα. All participants were nucleos(t)ide analogue-suppressed. Plasma samples were collected at three distinct time points: baseline, week 12, and week 24, providing a longitudinal view of how the proteome evolved in response to each therapy. The researchers performed longitudinal plasma proteomic profiling using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Of the proteins measured, seventy-seven passed the quality-control criteria and were included in the final analysis. The study employed linear mixed-effects models to analyze longitudinal protein changes. The primary results indicated that PEG-IFNα induced substantially broader longitudinal proteomic remodeling compared to PD-1 blockade. Most of the significant protein changes in the PEG-IFNα group occurred within the first 12 weeks of treatment. In contrast, the PD-1 blockade group showed a more limited range of proteomic shifts. Treatment-by-time analyses revealed distinct trajectories for the two therapies, highlighting differential changes in several key inflammatory markers, including IL-18R1, TNF, CX3CL1, CXCL9, and CXCL10. The researchers also evaluated the association between these proteomic changes and clinical response, defined as a decline in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) of at least one log10 IU/mL by week 24. Using responder–non-responder comparisons and Spearman’s rank correlation, the team identified treatment-specific patterns linked to this favorable decline. In the PD-1 blockade cohort, IL-10 emerged as the leading exploratory signal associated with HBsAg decline. In the PEG-IFNα cohort, IL-12B, CDCP1, and FGF-21 were more prominent in the response-associated analyses. However, the study emphasizes that these response-related associations did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction. Consequently, the authors classified these findings as exploratory rather than definitive biomarkers. The findings support the potential value of longitudinal proteomics for mechanistic and biomarker studies of HBV functional-cure strategies. By demonstrating that favorable HBsAg decline is accompanied by treatment-specific rather than universal proteomic signatures, the research highlights the potential value of tracking dynamic immune changes over time. Limitations of the study include the relatively small sample size, with only ten patients in the PD-1 blockade group and fifteen in the PEG-IFNα group. The research, published in Discover Medicine, indicates that this dual infection is associated with specific abnormalities in liver and kidney function markers, differentiating these patients from those infected with HIV alone. The study aimed to determine the biochemical characteristics of this co-infected population to better understand the physiological impact of the combined viral infections on overall patient health. The study was carried out at the Medical Analysis Laboratory of the Sino-Gabonese Cooperation Hospital in Libreville from August 1 to November 30, 2025. It included men and women aged 16 years and older who presented for serological testing for HIV and hepatitis B, along with a biochemical profile. Patients who were already on antiretroviral therapy were excluded from the analysis, as such treatment can significantly affect lipid levels, liver enzymes, and renal markers. The study population consisted of individuals of various nationalities, with some being sexually active and others not. Discover more healthy Get Health Tips health Out of 560 patients who tested positive for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, 60 were found to be positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), representing a prevalence of 10.71% within this specific cohort. The co-infected group was predominantly female, with 40 patients (66.67%) being women and 20 patients (33.33%) being men. The mean age of the co-infected patients was 36 years, with the most represented age group being 17 to 33 years. Socio-professionally, entrepreneurs constituted the largest group, followed by traders. Discover more Check Symptoms Get Tested infections infection The researchers analyzed several biochemical parameters, including glucose, uric acid, creatinine, urea, cholesterol, triglycerides, transaminases, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Blood samples were collected in dry tubes and centrifuged to obtain serum for analysis. The screening for HBsAg was performed using immunochromatographic tests and confirmed with the MINI VIDAS® automated assay. Biochemical parameters were determined using spectrophotometric methods on a SELECTRA PROS analyzer, ensuring precise measurement of the various serum components. The results revealed that co-infected patients exhibited significantly elevated levels of several key markers compared to reference values and the HIV-positive control group. Alkaline phosphatase levels were markedly high at 629.16 ± 9.88 IU/L, while gamma-glutamyl transferase levels were 70.66 ± 5.66 IU/L. Direct bilirubin was elevated at 14.15 ± 3.94 μmol/L, and total bilirubin was 20.05 ± 2.83 μmol/L. These findings suggest a cholestatic profile, which is characterized by the elevation of ALP, GGT, and bilirubin, indicating potential disruption in bile flow or liver function. Renal function markers also showed significant abnormalities in the co-infected group. Creatinine levels were notably high, with women averaging 199.65 ± 5.51 μmol/L and men averaging 245.68 ± 4.54 μmol/L. Urea levels were also elevated at 10.04 ± 1.15 mmol/L, although the p-value for this specific comparison was 0.25. The elevation of creatinine and urea suggests that the co-infection may have a synergistic effect on renal function, potentially leading to reduced kidney performance in these patients. In contrast to the elevated liver and renal markers, the study observed a significant decrease in total cholesterol levels among co-infected patients, with a mean of 2.81 ± 0.17 mmol/L. This hypocholesterolemia was significantly greater in co-infected patients than in those with HIV monoinfection, whose cholesterol levels were relatively normal. The researchers suggested that this decrease could be linked to the rapid progression of liver failure, such as cirrhosis, which is often associated with lower cholesterol levels in severely infected individuals. Discover more Study Biology Buy Maps Shop African Art Explore History Healthcare Interestingly, the levels of transaminases, specifically alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), were found to be within normal ranges for the co-infected patients. ALT levels were 20.05 ± 3.96 IU/L, and AST levels were 31.70 ± 8.86 IU/L. This finding contrasts with the typical expectation of elevated transaminases in liver disease. The authors explained that HIV-induced immunosuppression may limit the release of these liver enzymes into the blood, as the destruction of CD4+ T lymphocytes reduces the immune response that typically attacks HBV-infected hepatocytes. The study also noted that blood sugar levels were relatively normal in both co-infected and mono-infected patients, with a mean of 5.93 ± 0.66 mmol/L. Uric acid levels were increased in men compared to women, but co-infected men had GGT and urea levels that were closer to the healthy range compared to other groups. These observations highlight the complex interplay between the two viruses and their impact on various biochemical pathways in the body. The researchers acknowledged several limitations in the study, including the insufficient sample size, which was constrained by the high cost of laboratory reagents. They noted that a larger sample, ideally between 1,500 and 2,000 patients, would have provided more robust data. Additionally, the study did not measure IgM and anti-HBc antibodies to distinguish between acute and chronic infections, nor did it assess viral load or its impact on biochemical variations. Factors such as hepatitis C, delta virus, alcohol consumption, and hepatotoxic medications were not evaluated, which could have influenced the enzyme levels. The findings underscore the importance of monitoring biochemical parameters in patients with HIV-HBV coinfection. The distinct profile of hyperbilirubinemia, hypercreatinemia, and hypocholesterolemia suggests that these patients may be more vulnerable to hepatic and renal complications. The authors concluded that antiretroviral therapy should be accompanied by careful monitoring of these biochemical markers to manage the potential deterioration in overall health. This study provides valuable insights into the physiological effects of co-infection and highlights the need for tailored clinical approaches in managing these patients. Published in Discover Medicine, this research contributes to the growing body of evidence on the management of HIV-HBV coinfection. By identifying specific biochemical abnormalities, the study offers a framework for clinicians to better monitor and treat patients with this dual infection. The results emphasize the complexity of the disease and the necessity for comprehensive care that addresses both the viral and the metabolic aspects of the condition. To provide broader epidemiological context for their investigation, the researchers highlighted that human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B virus share major transmission pathways, including exposure to infected blood, sexual contact, and mother-to-child transmission. According to figures from the World Health Organization cited in the report, approximately 2.7 million individuals living with hepatitis B are co-infected with HIV, while an estimated 7.4 percent of people living with HIV globally also carry HBV. The authors noted that in the human body, urea serves as a marker of residual nitrogen generated through protein metabolism, reflecting renal filtration performance, while creatinine measures muscle breakdown products in circulation. Similarly, bilirubin functions as a bile pigment derived from hemoglobin catabolism that contributes antioxidant cellular protection, and alkaline phosphatase plays essential biological roles in both hepatic activity and bone formation. The study protocol incorporated specific diagnostic workflows and analytical assays to confirm infections and evaluate serum chemistry. Screening for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies utilized the Abbott Determine immunochromatographic rapid test, recognized for 100 percent sensitivity and 99.72 percent specificity, followed by confirmation with the automated MINI VIDAS system. Surface antigen detection for hepatitis B was performed using the ONSITE HBsAg Combo immunoassay, exhibiting up to 100 percent sensitivity and specificity, and similarly confirmed by automated VIDAS testing. Biochemical determinations on the SELECTRA PROS analyzer relied on standardized enzymatic chemistries: glucose, uric acid, creatinine, and cholesterol were evaluated via enzymatic PAP end-point techniques, urea was measured through urease and glutamate dehydrogenase kinetics, and transaminases were assessed using kinetic formulations without pyridoxal phosphate in line with established international clinical chemistry recommendations. In interpreting the distinct enzymatic patterns observed in co-infected patients, the investigators contextualized their findings using established diagnostic models of liver injury. Clinical frameworks categorize hepatic enzyme elevations into hepatocellular patterns marked primarily by increased transaminases, cholestatic patterns defined by raised alkaline phosphatase and hyperbilirubinemia, and mixed injury patterns displaying elevations across all three markers. The data showed that co-infected patients predominantly exhibited a cholestatic profile alongside elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase, whereas HIV mono-infected patients more frequently presented with mixed enzyme disruptions. The authors noted that the immunotolerant phase of hepatitis B infection, coupled with HIV-mediated depletion of CD4 positive T lymphocytes, diminishes cytotoxic immune destruction of HBV-infected hepatocytes, which keeps circulating transaminase concentrations deceptively low despite ongoing hepatobiliary disturbance. The demographic findings were also compared with regional surveillance data from across the African continent. The co-infected cohort had an overall mean age of 36.83 years, spanning an age range from 17 to 62 years, which closely aligns with cohorts evaluated in Nigeria and Cameroon. Addressing the two-to-one female predominance in their sample, the authors highlighted recognized biological, structural, and socio-economic vulnerabilities, including larger mucosal surface area and heightened anatomical susceptibility, that contribute to multiple viral acquisitions among women. Furthermore, while earlier Gabonese research in Franceville had documented higher coinfection frequencies in men, the Libreville results mirrored gender patterns reported in Guinea and broader population trends where women represent a larger share of individuals living with HIV. analysis_en.event: A prospective, cross-sectional study identified a distinct biochemical profile in patients co-infected with HIV and HBV, published in Discover Medicine by Bioengineer.org.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Out of 560 HIV-positive patients, 60 were co-infected with HBV (10.71%). The co-infected group showed elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, direct and total bilirubin, creatinine, and urea, while total cholesterol was significantly decreased. These findings suggest a cholestatic profile and potential renal dysfunction, with implications for clinical management.

news.title_zh: HIV-HBV 混合感染与加蓬独特的生化特征有关 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A study conducted in Libreville, Gabon, from August 1 to November 30, 2025, identified a distinct biochemical profile in patients co-infected with HIV and HBV. Published in Discover Medicine by Bioengineer.org, the research found that co-infected individuals had elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, direct and total bilirubin, creatinine, and urea, while total cholesterol was significantly lower. These results suggest a cholestatic profile and possible renal dysfunction, which may be linked to the synergistic effects of the dual infection. The study excluded patients on antiretroviral therapy and noted that transaminase levels were within normal ranges, possibly due to HIV-induced immunosuppression. The researchers emphasized the importance of monitoring these markers in co-infected patients to manage potential health deterioration. The findings are based on a specific cohort and do not indicate a public health outbreak.

Innovation Vir's Monthly Hepatitis Delta Combination Made the Virus Undetectable in 79% of Patients in Phase 3 Trial Published Nov 11, 2026 2:35 AM EST By Joseph James howan Sulaiman Ali / Middle East Images | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp A monthly two-drug injection made hepatitis delta virus undetectable in 79% of patients after 48 weeks in a phase 3 trial, Vir Biotechnology announced Nov. 9 at The Liver Meeting in Denver. None of the patients in a comparison group waiting to start treatment reached that result, according to the company's announcement. The trial's main goal was stricter. Undetectable virus combined with normal liver enzyme levels was reached by 44% of treated patients, compared with 0% in the delayed group. The results come from the company and have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal. The stakes are high for a small, often overlooked group. Hepatitis delta infects only people who already have hepatitis B, and it is considered the most severe form of viral hepatitis. The FDA approved the first U.S. treatment for it, Gilead's bulevirtide, in May. Inside the ECLIPSE 1 Results ECLIPSE 1 enrolled 124 adults with chronic hepatitis delta, including patients with compensated cirrhosis. They were randomly assigned two to one to start the combination of elebsiran and tobevibart right away, or to wait 12 weeks before starting. The comparison is not a standard placebo test, and that matters for reading the numbers. Treated patients were measured at week 48, while the delayed group was measured at week 12, before it began therapy. That design shows the drugs work against untreated infection, but it does not compare equal lengths of time. The trial was also open-label, meaning patients and doctors knew who was being treated, according to the study's ClinicalTrials.gov listing. Viral load is a lab measurement, which limits the risk of bias for that result, but it remains a design limit. The virus became undetectable in 85% of 46 treated patients with cirrhosis and 73% of 37 without it, Clinical Trials Arena reported. Liver enzyme levels returned to normal in 53% of treated patients, compared with 5% in the delayed group, according to the company. A Two-Drug Attack on Shared Viral Machinery Elebsiran is a small interfering RNA, a type of drug that silences genetic instructions the hepatitis B virus uses to make its surface protein. Hepatitis delta depends on that protein to build new virus particles and infect liver cells. Tobevibart is a monoclonal antibody, a lab-made immune protein that targets the hepatitis B surface protein. Together, the drugs attack machinery that both viruses need. Participants also took standard hepatitis B antiviral pills. "Our ambition in hepatitis D has always been to fundamentally change what patients can expect from treatment," said Vir CEO Marianne De Backer, Clinical Trials Arena reported. Evidence Check and Safety The company said the regimen was well tolerated. One patient had a severe, grade 3 drop in a type of white blood cell that resolved in 15 days, and no patients stopped or interrupted treatment. The most common side effect was flu-like symptoms, mostly after the first dose and usually gone within one to two days. The results do not yet show whether undetectable virus prevents cirrhosis, liver cancer, or death over years, or whether the effect lasts after treatment stops. Participants are scheduled to receive the drugs for up to 240 weeks, so longer-term data on liver outcomes should follow, though years of injections would also bring cost and access questions. In an earlier phase 2 study, all 10 patients in a small group who stopped after 96 weeks of suppression stayed suppressed 12 weeks later, but that group was tiny, and follow-up was short. Vir funded the trial and reported all figures. Independent experts have not yet reviewed the full data. The FDA has granted the combination Breakthrough Therapy and Fast Track designations, which can speed development and review but do not guarantee approval. Testing, Access and What Comes Next The people most likely to benefit are adults with chronic hepatitis B who also carry hepatitis delta, many of whom do not know it. In the United States, only about 8.5% to 12% of people with hepatitis B have been tested for delta in reported studies, according to a clinical review. Risk is higher among people who inject drugs and people from regions where the virus is common. People with hepatitis B can ask their clinician whether they have been tested for hepatitis delta, which starts with a blood antibody test. Those diagnosed can ask about referral to a liver specialist, about bulevirtide, which received accelerated FDA approval in May as a daily injection, and about clinical trials. Hepatitis B vaccination also prevents hepatitis delta, because the delta virus cannot infect someone without hepatitis B. Adults who are not vaccinated can ask a pharmacist or clinician about the series. Yellowing of the skin or eyes, a swollen belly, confusion or vomiting blood need urgent care. Vir plans to seek FDA approval in mid-2027. Results from ECLIPSE 2, which tests switching patients who did not respond to bulevirtide, and ECLIPSE 3, a head-to-head comparison with bulevirtide, are expected in early 2027. Price has not been announced. MedicalDaily will report the full publication and the FDA filing. The trial, named ECLIPSE 1, enrolled 124 adults with chronic hepatitis delta, including those with compensated cirrhosis. Patients were randomly assigned to start treatment immediately or wait 12 weeks. At week 48, 79% of treated patients had undetectable virus levels, compared to 0% in the delayed group. Additionally, 44% of treated patients reached normal liver enzyme levels, while the comparison group had no such results. The findings, reported by Vir and not yet published in a peer-reviewed journal, highlight the potential of the treatment for this small, often overlooked group. The trial also included standard hepatitis B antiviral pills as part of the regimen. These results are significant as hepatitis delta is considered the most severe form of viral hepatitis and infects only people who already have hepatitis B.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Study Identifies Predictors of Antiviral Treatment Failure in HBV and HCV Coinfection by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Study Identifies Predictors of Antiviral Treatment Failure in HBV and HCV Coinfection Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Direct-acting antiviral treatment achieved high rates of viral clearance among patients coinfected with hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses, according to a retrospective cohort study evaluating treatment outcomes and predictive models in Pakistan. The investigation focused on identifying baseline clinical, virological, and liver-fibrosis indicators that anticipate both early and sustained treatment non-response. While dual infection has historically complicated therapeutic management in endemic regions, twelve weeks of combined sofosbuvir and daclatasvir yielded sustained clearance in the clear majority of treated individuals. The clinical evaluation took place at Holy Family Hospital in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, and enrolled a cohort of 207 adult patients diagnosed with concurrent hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections. Every participant underwent a standard 12-week therapeutic regimen consisting of the direct-acting antiviral agents sofosbuvir and daclatasvir. To examine the trajectory of viral persistence, the researchers recorded all potential host and viral predictors prior to the start of treatment, establishing a rigorous baseline to evaluate subsequent therapeutic outcomes. Therapeutic success and failure were measured across two distinct post-treatment observation milestones. The research team defined sustained virological response failure at week four, designated as SVR4 failure, as the presence of detectable hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid four weeks following the completion of therapy. Similarly, sustained virological response failure at week twelve, termed SVR12 failure, was defined as detectable viral ribonucleic acid measured twelve weeks post-treatment, serving as the benchmark for sustained therapeutic non-response. Primary outcome measurements demonstrated robust overall efficacy across the cohort despite the presence of complex dual viral infections. Sustained virological response at four weeks was achieved by 186 out of 207 patients, representing an early response rate of 89.9 percent, whereas 21 patients, or 10.1 percent, experienced SVR4 failure. By the twelve-week post-treatment mark, sustained virological response was confirmed in 175 individuals, corresponding to an 84.5 percent success rate, while 32 participants, or 15.5 percent of the cohort, experienced SVR12 failure. To uncover the variables linked to therapeutic non-response, the investigators performed univariable screening alongside exploratory multivariable logistic regression analyses. For early non-response at four weeks, multivariable modeling demonstrated that SVR4 failure was independently associated with a higher body mass index, higher baseline hepatitis C viral RNA levels, and male sex. In contrast, patient history or status with an interferon-based regimen was associated with lower adjusted odds of experiencing treatment failure at this early post-treatment benchmark. Multivariable evaluation of twelve-week outcomes identified overlapping and distinct clinical determinants associated with long-term viral clearance. SVR12 failure was significantly associated with older patient age, elevated body mass index, male sex, and higher pre-treatment viral load levels. Consistent with the four-week findings, status involving an interferon-containing therapeutic regimen was again associated with lower adjusted odds of therapeutic failure at the twelve-week evaluation point. Beyond conventional regression, the study deployed internally validated machine learning models developed separately to predict four-week and twelve-week outcomes. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, precision-recall area under the curve metrics, and SHAP feature importance analysis. The XGBoost algorithm achieved the highest precision-recall area under the curve for predicting SVR4 failure, whereas the Random Forest algorithm attained the highest precision-recall area under the curve for predicting SVR12 failure. SHAP interpretation highlighted pre-treatment viral RNA levels, patient age, body mass index, and fibrosis indices as the primary contributors guiding model predictions. Although fibrosis-related variables contributed substantially to descriptive observations and machine learning interpretations, the study authors emphasized that these predictive algorithms remain exploratory and require rigorous external validation in independent clinical cohorts before direct implementation in routine hepatitis care. news.title: Ghana Prison Study Finds High HBV Infectivity Markers
news.excerpt: A cross-sectional study of 323 HBsAg-positive inmates in Ghana found that 28.2% had markers of high HBV infectivity and 5.0% had markers of recent infection.

The study, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, examined 323 samples from inmates who tested positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen, commonly known as HBsAg. The research aimed to evaluate the presence of hepatitis B e antigen, or HBeAg, and immunoglobulin M antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen, referred to as anti-HBc IgM, within this specific population. Correctional facilities are often recognized as high-risk environments for the transmission of blood-borne infections due to factors such as overcrowding, high-risk behaviors, and limited access to healthcare services. The study was conducted as a secondary analysis, utilizing data and biological samples collected during a nationwide prison survey. The researchers focused on a cohort of 323 individuals who had previously been identified as HBsAg-positive. The laboratory methods employed in this analysis involved enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays, or ELISAs, to detect the presence of HBeAg and anti-HBc IgM in the archived plasma samples. The results of the analysis revealed that 91 out of the 323 HBsAg-positive samples, representing 28.2 percent, were positive for HBeAg. This finding indicates that more than a quarter of the HBsAg-positive inmates in the study had serological evidence of increased viral infectivity. Additionally, 16 samples, or 5.0 percent, tested positive for anti-HBc IgM. This smaller proportion suggests that a subset of the population may have experienced recent infection or a reactivation of chronic disease. The statistical analysis further showed that HBeAg positivity was significantly associated with the type of prison and the duration of incarceration, with p-values less than 0.001 and 0.05, respectively. Regarding the anti-HBc IgM marker, the study found that most inmates who tested positive for this antibody had been incarcerated for more than one year. However, the researchers noted that no significant associations were observed between anti-HBc IgM positivity and the demographic variables examined in the study. The study design, being cross-sectional, has inherent limitations that the authors carefully addressed in their conclusion. In this context, the absence of pre-incarceration serological data precludes the confirmation that transmission occurred specifically within the prison. Although these findings highlight the potential for HBV transmission within correctional facilities, the cross-sectional design and absence of pre-incarceration serological data preclude confirmation of intra-prison transmission. The study suggests that strengthened HBV screening, vaccination programs, and clinical management are warranted to mitigate the risk of transmission. Furthermore, the researchers recommend longitudinal studies that incorporate HBV DNA testing to better characterize the dynamics of HBV transmission in correctional settings. Regarding the anti-HBc IgM marker, the study found that most inmates who tested positive for this antibody had been incarcerated for more than one year. However, the researchers noted that no significant associations were observed between anti-HBc IgM positivity and the demographic variables examined in the study. The study design, being cross-sectional, has inherent limitations that the authors carefully addressed in their conclusion. In this context, the absence of pre-incarceration serological data precludes the confirmation that transmission occurred specifically within the prison. Although these findings highlight the potential for HBV transmission within correctional facilities, the cross-sectional design and absence of pre-incarceration serological data preclude confirmation of intra-prison transmission. The study suggests that strengthened HBV screening, vaccination programs, and clinical management are warranted to mitigate the risk of transmission. Furthermore, the researchers recommend longitudinal studies that incorporate HBV DNA testing to better characterize the dynamics of HBV transmission in correctional settings. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Systematic Review Identifies Hepatitis C as Pakistan’s Primary Liver Cancer Driver by November 11, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Systematic Review Identifies Hepatitis C as Pakistan's Primary Liver Cancer Driver Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A systematic review evaluating thirty-five years of clinical and epidemiological data has identified hepatitis C virus as the primary etiological driver of hepatocellular carcinoma in Pakistan, far outpacing hepatitis B virus and alcohol consumption. Hepatocellular carcinoma represents the predominant primary liver cancer worldwide, accounting for seventy-five to eighty-five percent of hepatic malignancies and ranking as the sixth leading cause of cancer mortality. In 2022, approximately 865,269 new cases and 757,948 deaths occurred globally. In Pakistan, disease incidence has climbed steadily, placing liver cancer among the most frequently diagnosed malignancies in adult males. The new qualitative synthesis integrates evidence from ninety-eight clinical studies published between 1990 and 2025 to delineate national disease trends and viral contributions across diverse Pakistani patient populations and healthcare settings. Pathologically, hepatocellular carcinoma develops after protracted hepatic damage and extensive cirrhosis caused by viral infections, alcohol, or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Within cirrhotic tissue, dysplastic macronodules progressively advance into early hepatocellular carcinoma through multi-step hepatocarcinogenesis before progressing to advanced stages. In rare instances, tumors develop within healthy liver tissue, possibly arising from malignant transformation of hepatocellular adenomas. Clinical tumor detection relies heavily on elevated alpha-fetoprotein serum biomarkers across regional medical centers. Because underlying cirrhosis remains asymptomatic in most patients, early diagnosis proves challenging, resulting in delayed clinical presentation and increased mortality. Over the course of malignant progression, the diseased liver progressively loses its capacity to maintain enzymatic balance, ultimately culminating in fatal systemic failure unless appropriate clinical intervention occurs promptly in specialized tertiary hospitals. Discover more Read Med Journals Study Biology Find Treatments To clarify national trends, investigators conducted their analysis following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines under prospective PROSPERO registration number CRD42023442582. The research protocol applied the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome framework, designating the Pakistani population as the study group and evaluating exposures to hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, viral co-infection, and alcohol consumption to assess their relative contributions. The primary measured outcome was the occurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma across patient cohorts. The review authors executed an extensive literature search across ScienceDirect, PubMed, Google Scholar, Springer, and BMC from January 2022 through March 2025, evaluating English-language studies published between 1990 and 2025 using tailored Boolean expressions, Medical Subject Headings, and manual reference screening of eligible articles to ensure comprehensive retrieval. Discover more Find Cancer Care Check Symptoms cancer Cancer Database searches initially identified 539 citations, which underwent rigorous multi-stage eligibility screening. After removing 122 duplicate publications, title and abstract evaluations excluded 263 irrelevant articles. Full-text assessments were performed on 158 candidate studies, of which 57 were eliminated for lacking sufficient data aligned with review objectives, leaving 98 eligible studies involving advanced-stage disease cohorts. A formal quantitative meta-analysis was initially considered to determine pooled prevalence figures; however, substantial methodological heterogeneity precluded statistical aggregation. The included investigations showed wide discrepancies in study design, sample sizes, patient selection, diagnostic criteria, and geographic coverage, while several reports provided qualitative findings without numerical numerators and denominators necessary for pooled estimation, prompting a descriptive qualitative systematic review approach instead of a formal statistical meta-analysis. Methodological quality across the 98 incorporated studies was evaluated using the Quality in Prognostic Studies tool across six standard domains: study participation, study attrition, prognostic factor measurement, outcome measurement, confounding account, and statistical analysis. Overall, 41 studies exhibited low risk of bias, 38 moderate risk, and 19 high risk. Prognostic factor and outcome assessments demonstrated the lowest risk of bias because most studies employed established diagnostic standards for hepatic malignancy and viral infections. Conversely, confounding measurement showed the highest proportion of moderate-to-high risk ratings due to inadequate adjustment for age, sex, diabetes mellitus, and cirrhosis severity. These statistical reporting limitations and retrospective designs yielded an overall moderate confidence in the evidence, requiring cautious interpretation across regional healthcare settings. Among evaluated causes, chronic hepatitis C virus infection proved to be the primary cause of liver cancer across Pakistan, examined across 32 included studies. Globally, hepatitis C affects roughly 71.1 million people, but in Pakistan the blood-borne RNA virus maintains hyper-endemic transmission that imposes an immense clinical and economic toll. Transmission occurs primarily through contaminated blood products, unsafe medical injections, and inadequate equipment sterilization during healthcare procedures. With approximately 1.5 million blood donations collected annually in Pakistan, rigorous donor screening remains central to transmission control, particularly given estimated hepatitis C prevalence of 3.31 percent plus or minus 1.96 percent among healthy blood donors. Of the 32 dedicated hepatitis C studies, 21 confirmed that chronic infection induced hepatocellular carcinoma, 8 observed the highest incidence from hepatitis C, and only 3 reported a low incidence. Geographical analyses across Pakistan revealed pronounced regional differences in viral hepatitis and cancer distribution. Southern Pakistan showed hepatitis C and hepatitis B population prevalence rates of 1.84 percent and 1.7 percent, whereas northern areas recorded 1.3 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively. Center-specific studies reflected these patterns: Islamabad’s Nuclear Medicine Oncology and Radiotherapy Institute found 44.7 percent of liver cancer patients positive for hepatitis C, 13.1 percent for hepatitis B, and 4.3 percent co-infected. In Lahore, Shaikh Zayed Postgraduate Medical Institute observed hepatitis C in 75 percent, hepatitis B in 10 percent, and co-infection in 10 percent. Multan recorded 80 percent hepatitis C and 11 percent hepatitis B, while Muzaffargarh reported 67.3 percent hepatitis C, 5.9 percent hepatitis B, and 7.9 percent co-infection. Additional regional data illustrated continued hepatitis C predominance in northwest and southern centers alongside distinct localized exceptions. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, provincial research showed that 77.78 percent of liver cancer patients carried hepatitis C, 17.78 percent had viral co-infection, and only 4.44 percent had isolated hepatitis B. In Sindh, combined data from Isra University Hospital and Liaquat University Hospital in Hyderabad demonstrated 72.5 percent hepatitis C, 21.0 percent hepatitis B, 10.5 percent concurrent alcoholic liver disease with hepatitis C, and 6.5 percent viral co-infections. In Baluchistan, 7.5 percent of evaluated tumor patients had prior exposure to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or co-infection. Conversely, Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre in Karachi documented hepatitis B in 67 percent of cancer patients and hepatitis C in 33 percent, demonstrating substantial epidemiological heterogeneity across geographic regions. Twenty included studies specifically evaluated hepatitis B virus contributions to hepatocellular carcinoma across the country. Globally, hepatitis B affects approximately 284 million individuals, with associated annual mortality climbing from 580,500 deaths in 1990 to 799,000 deaths by 2017. Although national blood donor surveys show donor hepatitis B prevalence between 2.41 percent and 1.96 percent, reflecting a gradual reduction, specific districts in northern Pakistan exhibit substantial endemicity. Reported regional rates include 13.35 percent in Mardan, 13.5 percent in Bannu, 14.15 percent in Peshawar, 14.15 percent in Kohat, 14.63 percent in Dera Ismail Khan, and 16.35 percent in Malakand. Among the 20 evaluated hepatitis B studies, 13 confirmed chronic infection induction, 5 reported it as the primary cause, and 2 noted low incidence, reflecting an epidemiological transition from earlier decades when hepatitis B predominated. Viral co-infection was examined in 20 studies, demonstrating that dual hepatitis B and hepatitis C exposure causes severe disease burdens. Multiple clinical cohorts documented significant co-infection proportions: Butt and colleagues identified 10 percent co-infection alongside 5 percent non-viral cases, while Farooqi and Farooqi recorded 17.78 percent. Other cohorts observed co-infection frequencies ranging from 2.44 percent to 10.3 percent, occasionally alongside hepatitis D or non-B non-C etiologies. Long-term demographic forecasts by Zahoor and colleagues projected hepatitis B and hepatitis C infection prevalence rates of approximately 3.25 percent and 6.36 percent by 2030. These ongoing projections indicate that sustained viral circulation will continue to fuel chronic liver disease and primary liver cancer across Pakistan without enhanced clinical intervention, expanded screening programs, and active patient surveillance. In sharp contrast to Western cohorts where alcohol abuse represents a major cause of liver malignancy, alcohol-induced hepatocellular carcinoma remains exceptionally rare in Pakistan. Only six studies evaluated alcohol, with Khan and colleagues reporting that merely 2 percent of cancer patients had an alcohol history, despite general observations that regular alcohol intake increases cancer risk by approximately 6 percent. Low alcohol-associated frequencies were consistently observed across three studies from Lahore and two from Sindh, while a Peshawar cohort identified alcohol-related disease in 3.2 percent of cases. Concurrently, emerging non-viral risks including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and dietary aflatoxin B1 exposure causing TP53 gene mutations represent recognized global carcinogens, but empirical clinical research systematically evaluating their contribution in Pakistan remains remarkably scarce. Regarding clinical management, a subset of included studies reported interventions across tertiary medical centers, encompassing surgical resection, liver transplantation, local ablation, transarterial procedures, and systemic pharmacological therapies. Surgical intervention constituted the most frequently utilized therapeutic modality, documented in 1,820 managed cases, alongside microwave ablation, radiofrequency ablation, transarterial chemoembolization, transarterial radioembolization, and systemic drugs such as sorafenib, lenvatinib, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. However, treatment reporting varied substantially across published literature, frequently omitting tumor staging, allocation guidelines, and survival outcomes, while access to liver transplantation and advanced immunotherapy remains geographically constrained. Review authors concluded that addressing referral bias, establishing comprehensive national cancer registries, expanding hepatitis B vaccination, and widening direct-acting antiviral coverage will be critical to mitigating the expanding burden of hepatocellular carcinoma in Pakistan.
